overview: Anhalt comprised related central German principalities before their territories were united as a duchy in 1863. Its courts supported language scholarship, music and landscape design, while its later republican history included experiments in housing. These changing states were predecessors of part of modern Saxony-Anhalt, not the whole modern state under an earlier name.

periods.title: Related but separate principalities
periods.summary: Anhalt was divided into Bernburg, Dessau, Köthen and Zerbst. Some responsibilities, including mining and the common archive, remained jointly organized.

periods.title: Language scholarship at Köthen
periods.summary: The Fruitbearing Society developed a network of correspondence and literary discussion under Prince Ludwig. Its work included translation, criticism and questions of German usage.

periods.title: Bach at the Köthen court
periods.summary: Johann Sebastian Bach served Prince Leopold as court music director from 1717 to 1723. His employment connects the small principality with the wider history of European music.

periods.title: A landscape for education and daily work
periods.summary: Wörlitz brought architecture, agricultural land and public learning into a designed landscape. A new synagogue, built in 1789 to 1790, served the town’s Jewish community.

periods.title: The united duchy
periods.summary: The extinction of ruling branches in Köthen and Bernburg brought their territories together with Dessau. The resulting Duchy of Anhalt retained its own government.

periods.title: Republican institutions
periods.summary: The ducal house renounced the throne in November 1918. Elections and a new legislature followed; Marie Kettmann entered the parliament in December 1919.

periods.title: Experimental housing at Dessau
periods.summary: The Törten estate tested serial construction and small household gardens as answers to housing needs. The foundation’s account also records limits to affordability.

periods.title: Absorbed into a larger administration
periods.summary: Under Soviet occupation, Anhalt became part of a new Province of Saxony in 1945. This was subsequently renamed Saxony-Anhalt and became a Land in 1947.

items.text: Anhalt’s partitions did not eliminate all common institutions. The senior reigning prince handled shared business such as its imperial parliamentary voice, mining and the joint archive. These arrangements help explain why one regional name can cover several courts and administrations; the map’s broad label should not imply a permanently unified state.

The Fruitbearing Society’s Köthen correspondence discussed translations, literary style and vocabulary. The scholarly edition describes a 1624 discussion that accepted an established borrowed word instead of replacing it with proposed alternatives. This makes language planning visible as argument and choice, rather than a single ruler’s invention of standard German.

Bach’s position at Köthen was an occupation within a princely household: he directed court music for Leopold from 1717 to 1723. The connection illustrates how a small court could support specialist artistic labor. It does not make every work associated with Bach an Anhalt composition or prove that all residents heard court performances.

Wörlitz Palace, built from 1769 to 1773, formed part of a landscape that also displayed farming methods and new bridge designs. UNESCO interprets the arrangement as both educational and economic. Fields and working buildings belonged to the project, so its meaning extends beyond ornamental gardens made for elite enjoyment.

The Wörlitz synagogue was built in 1789 to 1790 to designs by Friedrich Wilhelm von Erdmannsdorff. A ritual bath survives beneath the circular building. Its combined architectural form and religious provision make it evidence for a particular Jewish community’s worship, not simply a decorative temple placed in a park.

The synagogue’s furnishings were destroyed during the Nazi pogrom of 1938. Residents and garden director Hans Hallervorden helped prevent destruction of the building; he subsequently lost his post. The survival of the structure therefore cannot be read as evidence that the community or its religious life escaped persecution.

sections.title: Households and practical reform after the monarchy

items.text: Marie Kettmann, the wife of an Elbe boatman and a mother, entered Anhalt’s parliament in December 1919. Its account describes a reception still shaped by assumptions about women’s limited political role. Formal admission opened participation, while the language and behavior of the chamber show that equality in everyday parliamentary life remained contested.

Kettmann also reported on a petition concerning the choice of a midwife. The rules required a payment to the public treasury even when a family called an independent midwife. This specific dispute shows how parliamentary work could address household costs and childbirth, subjects easily missed in histories focused only on cabinets and rulers.

Dessau’s Törten estate combined repeated house designs with gardens for fruit, vegetables and small livestock. Haus Anton, built in 1926, retains its original arrangement, including a bathtub in the kitchen and space for animals. Such surviving fittings connect modern architecture with cooking, washing and supplementary food production in one household.

Standardization did not automatically make Törten cheap for workers. The Bauhaus foundation notes that furnishings offered for a model home were too expensive, and that the affordable-housing aim was better realized in Hannes Meyer’s later apartment buildings. The experiment’s ambition and its practical limitations are both part of its achievement.

On 12 November 1918, Prince Regent Aribert renounced the throne on behalf of the ducal house. A state council replaced ducal government and prepared elections. This was the end of Anhalt’s monarchy, not the disappearance of its inhabitants or immediate absorption of the territory into another state.

After the Second World War, Soviet occupation authorities combined Anhalt with the Magdeburg and Halle-Merseburg provinces in a new Province of Saxony. The archive distinguishes its 1945 formation, the Saxony-Anhalt name adopted in 1946 and Land status in 1947. Modern Saxony-Anhalt therefore has a different territorial and institutional history from the old duchy.

ending.text: Anhalt’s monarchy ended in 1918, while its separate territorial administration ended through postwar reorganization in 1945. Local communities, buildings and cultural traditions continued through those changes. The map’s 1878 cutoff is neither of these political endings.
